title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
1.1 Key concepts
Hypothesis testing is a fundamental concept in the scientific world. The purpose of hypothesis testing is to present a decision rule, established before using sample results, that allows a choice to be made between two statistical hypotheses.
What is a statistical hypothesis? It is an a priori statement about one or more characteristics of a population, such as the value of parameters or the distribution of observations.
There are two types of hypotheses:
What is type-I and type-II errors ?
Statistical power, it is the probability to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false. \(Power = 1 - \beta\)

title: 1  Théorie générale des tests statistiques
text:
Hypothèse nulle (H₀) : hypothèse soumise au test statistique et considérée comme vraie pour le test, H₀ est souvent un modèle simple ou bien une valeur définie d’un paramètre. Exemple, il n’y a pas de différence entre les moyennes de mes deux groupes, \(H_0\) : \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\)
Hypothèse alternative (H₁) : hypothèse différente de \(H_0\), communément son opposé. Exemple \(H_1\) : \(\mu_1 ≠ \mu_2\)



α l’erreur de Type I (ou risque de première espèce) : c’est la probabilité de rejeter H₀ alors que H₀ est vraie. Dit autrement, c’est le risque de conclure à tort, via les résultats obtenus, sur une différence réelle alors qu’elle est due au hasard. Exemple : un joueur joue à la roulette, il lance la roue 6 fois, il voit sortir 4 numéros rouges et 2 numéros noirs. Il en conclu qu’il y a deux fois plus de numéros rouges que de noirs.








Figure 1: example of the roulette game





β l’erreur de Type II (ou risque de deuxième espèce) : c’est la probabilité de ne pas rejeter H₀ alors que \(H_0\) est fausse. En autres, c’est le risque de conclure à tort qu’il n’y a pas de différence alors qu’il y a une différence réelle.

title: 1  Théorie générale des tests statistiques
text:
1.2 Test de Student (ou t test)
Le test de Student permet une comparaison simple mais importante, celle des moyennes entre deux groupes. La statistique de test est définie ainsi
\[
t = c \, \frac{\bar{m}_1 - \bar{m}_2}{s}
\]
Où \(\bar{m}_1\) et \(\bar{m}_2\) sont les moyennes respectives des deux groupes, \(c\) est une constante dépendante de la taille d’échantillon, \(s^{2}\) est l’estimateur sans biais de la variance globale. \[
\bar{m}_1 = \frac{1}{n_1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} x_{1,i}
\qquad
\bar{m}_2 = \frac{1}{n_2} \sum_{i=1}^{n_2} x_{2,i}
\]
\(s_1^2\) et \(s_2^2\) sont les estimateurs sans biais de la variance intra-groupe.
\[
s_1^2 = \frac{1}{n_1 - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} (x_{1,i} - \bar{m}_1)^2
\qquad
s_2^2 = \frac{1}{n_2 - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_2} (x_{2,i} - \bar{m}_2)^2
\]
\[
s =
\sqrt{
\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}
     {n_1 + n_2 - 2}
}
\]
\[
c = \sqrt{\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}}
\]




1.2.1 Test de Student à deux échantillons indépendants
Compare les moyennes de deux groupes indépendants : trt2 (n=10) et crtl (n=10).







Figure 2 : Exemple de données de deux groupes





tt <- with(exemple_data,
          t.test(weight[group =="ctrl"],
                 weight[group =="trt2"],
                 var.equal = TRUE))
tt

t = -2.134, df = 18, p-value = 0.04685
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.980338117 -0.007661883
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    5.032     5.526 


On observe une différence entre mes deux groupes de faible échantillon, que ce passerait-il si on augmente artificiellement la taille d’échantillon en dupliquant les données ? Je conserve le même groupe





Figure 3 : Graphique montrant l’évolution de la p-valeur (échelle log) en fonction de la taille d’échantillon par groupe.







    Two Sample t-test

data:  weight[group == "ctrl"] and weight[group == "trt2"]
t = -7.0777, df = 198, p-value = 2.483e-11
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.6316394 -0.3563606
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    5.032     5.526 


Dans cet exemple j’ai dupliqué dix fois le jeu de données, on peut voir que les moyennes sont identiques mais que la pvalue associée est bien plus basse :

La puissance statistique associée au test de Student est dépendante de la taille d’échantillon. Plus le nombre d’observations est élevé, plus les résultats seront significatifs.

text:
1.4 Test de proportion
Teste si une proportion observée diffère d’une proportion théorique.

# Exemple: 55 succès sur 100 essais
# H₀: p = 0.5 vs H₁: p ≠ 0.5
resultat_prop <- prop.test(x = 55, n = 100, p = 0.5)
print(resultat_prop)


    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  55 out of 100, null probability 0.5
X-squared = 0.81, df = 1, p-value = 0.3681
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.4475426 0.6485719
sample estimates:
   p 
0.55 

# Test de comparaison de deux proportions
# Groupe 1: 45/100, Groupe 2: 60/100
resultat_prop2 <- prop.test(x = c(45, 60), n = c(100, 100))
print(resultat_prop2)


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(45, 60) out of c(100, 100)
X-squared = 3.9298, df = 1, p-value = 0.04744
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.296847038 -0.003152962
sample estimates:
prop 1 prop 2

  groupe = c("Groupe 1", "Groupe 2"),

)

ggplot(prop_data, aes(x = groupe, y = proportion, fill = groupe)) +

title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
2.2 Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER)
Probability to get at least one false positive, knowing the true null hypotheses
FWER = P(at least one false positive) ou \(P(V>0 | m_0)\)
We want to stricly control number the number of false positives. Apply we \(m\) is pretty small.

2.2.1 Bonferroni method
Stricly control FWER. How it works ? Divide \(\alpha\) by number of test \(m\).
reject hypothesis if p-value \(< \alpha / m\)





Figure 7: FWER versus number of tests.





Exercise : Reproduce figure 7, \(m = 100\), \(\alpha = 0.05\).


2.2.2 Holm method
Method less conservative than Bonferonni, the main idea is make the significance threshold less strict as the p-values get larger
adjusted p-values : \(q_{(i)} = \min(1, \max_{j \le i}[(m + 1 - j) * p_{(j)} ])\)
Procedure:

Sort the p-values in ascending order
Compare the smallest p-value to \(\alpha / m\)
If the associated \(H_0\) is not rejected stop, otherwise continue
Compare the second smallest p-value to \(\alpha / m-1\)
If the associated \(H_0\) is not rejected stop, otherwise continue
Keep going till compare the largent p-value to \(\alpha\)
crumbs: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests

title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
2.3 False Discovery Rate (FDR)
FDR is the expected number of significant results which are false positive on average.
\(FDR = E(V/R)\) with \(V\) number of false positives (type-I error) ; \(R\) number of rejections \(V/R\) is called false discovery proportion (FDP)
We use the FDR when \(m\) is very large and the FWER is too conservative in this case.
We also need to control the FDR because the FDP increase if there is a lot of true negatives in comparison to true positives
Example with a test with \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(\beta\) = 1: I test 25 variables, 5 of which are true positives So we have 5 true positives and \(20*0.05\) (1) false positive \(FDP = 1/(5+1)\) \(= 16.67\%\)
Same test but with 505 variables and still 5 true positives So we have 5 true positives and \(500*0.05\) (25) false positives \(FDP = 25/(5+25)\) \(= 83.33\%\)

2.3.1 Benjamini-Hochberg method (B-H)
This method control the FDR and the main idea is similar to Holm’s correction Note that B-H requires independent assumptions or at least positively correlated between tests to garantee FDR control
adjusted p-values : \(q_{(i)} = \min(1, \min_{j \ge i}[(m / j) * p_{(j)} ])\)
Procedure with \(\alpha\) the desired FDR level:

Sort the p-values in ascending order
Compare the smallest p-value to \(\alpha / m\)
If the associated \(H_0\) is not rejected stop, otherwise continue
Compare the second smallest p-value to \(2\alpha / m\)
If the associated \(H_0\) is not rejected stop, otherwise continue
…
Keep rejecting \(H_0\) until the first \(p_{(i)} \ge \frac{i*\alpha}{m}\)
Do not reject the remaining hypotheses



2.3.2 Benjamini-Yekutieli method (B-Y)
B-Y is more conservative than B-H requires no assumptions on the test dependence structure.
adjusted p-values : \(q_{(i)} = \min(1, \min_{j \ge i}[\frac{m*\sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{k}}{j} * p_{(j)} ])\)
Similar procedure as B-H method except that the number of tests is inflated to account for possible dependencies

Sort the p-values in ascending order
Compare the smallest p-value to \(\alpha / (m * \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{k})\)
Compare the second smallest p-value to \(2\alpha / (m * \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{k})\)
…
Keep rejecting \(H_0\) until the first \(p_{(i)} \ge \frac{i*\alpha}{(m * \sum_{k=1}^{m} \frac{1}{k})}\)
Do not reject the remaining hypotheses



2.3.3 Methods comparison

title: 1  Théorie générale des tests statistiques
text:
2.4 Corrections pour tests multiples

# Générer des p-values de test
set.seed(123)
n_tests <- 100
# 90 vrais H₀ (non significatifs) et 10 vrais H₁ (significatifs)
p_vals <- c(
  runif(90, 0.05, 1),  # vrais négatifs
  runif(10, 0, 0.01)   # vrais positifs
)
p_vals <- sample(p_vals)  # mélanger


2.4.1 Correction de Holm (Bonferroni séquentielle)
Version moins conservative de Bonferroni.

p_holm <- p.adjust(p_vals, method = "holm")

cat("Tests significatifs (Holm):", sum(p_holm < alpha), "\n")

Tests significatifs (Holm): 0 




2.4.2 False Discovery Rate (Benjamini-Hochberg)
Contrôle le FDR au lieu du FWER, plus puissant pour les tests multiples.

p_fdr <- p.adjust(p_vals, method = "BH")

cat("Tests significatifs (FDR/BH):", sum(p_fdr < alpha), "\n")

Tests significatifs (FDR/BH): 0 




2.4.3 Comparaison des méthodes

# Créer un tableau comparatif
comparaison <- data.frame(
  p_value = p_vals,
  rang = rank(p_vals),
  non_corrige = p_vals < alpha,
  holm = p_holm < alpha,
  BH_FDR = p_fdr < alpha
)

# Résumé
resume <- data.frame(
  Methode = c("Non corrigé", "Holm", "BH (FDR)"),
  Significatifs = c(
    sum(comparaison$non_corrige),
    sum(comparaison$holm),
    sum(comparaison$BH_FDR)
  )
)

print(resume)

      Methode Significatifs
1 Non corrigé            10
2        Holm             0
3    BH (FDR)             0

# Visualisation
comparaison_long <- comparaison %>%
  select(rang, non_corrige, holm, BH_FDR) %>%
  pivot_longer(-rang, names_to = "methode", values_to = "significatif") %>%
  mutate(methode = factor(methode, 
                          levels = c("non_corrige", "holm", "BH_FDR"),
                          labels = c("Non corrigé", "Holm", "BH (FDR)")))

ggplot(comparaison_long, aes(x = rang, y = methode, fill = significatif)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "darkgreen"), 
                    labels = c("Non significatif", "Significatif")) +
  labs(title = "Comparaison des méthodes de correction",
       x = "Rang de la p-value (1 = plus petite)",
       y = "Méthode",
       fill = "") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")










2.4.4 Visualisation des seuils de décision

# Créer un dataframe pour la visualisation
df_viz <- data.frame(
  rang = 1:n_tests,
  p_value = sort(p_vals)
) %>%
  mutate(
    seuil_standard = alpha,
    seuil_bonferroni = alpha / n_tests,
    seuil_BH = (rang / n_tests) * alpha
  )

ggplot(df_viz, aes(x = rang)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = p_value), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = seuil_standard, color = "Standard (α = 0.05)"), 
            size = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = seuil_bonferroni, color = "Bonferroni"), 
            size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = seuil_BH, color = "Benjamini-Hochberg"), 
            size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "blue", "green")) +
  labs(title = "Seuils de décision selon les méthodes",
       x = "Rang de la p-value",
       y = "P-value",
       color = "Méthode") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: 1  Théorie générale des tests statistiques
text:
2.5 Recommandations pratiques

2.5.1 Choix de la méthode



Situation
Méthode recommandée




Nombre limité de tests (< 10)
Bonferroni


Besoin de contrôle strict du FWER
Bonferroni ou Holm


Grand nombre de tests
FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg)


Exploration de données
FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg)


Confirmation d’hypothèses
Bonferroni





2.5.2 Code récapitulatif

# Fonction pour comparer toutes les méthodes
comparer_corrections <- function(p_values, alpha = 0.05) {
  data.frame(
    Methode = c("Non corrigé", "Bonferroni", "Holm", "Hochberg", 
                "Hommel", "BH (FDR)", "BY (FDR)"),
    Significatifs = c(
      sum(p_values < alpha),
      sum(p.adjust(p_values, "bonferroni") < alpha),
      sum(p.adjust(p_values, "holm") < alpha),
      sum(p.adjust(p_values, "hochberg") < alpha),
      sum(p.adjust(p_values, "hommel") < alpha),
      sum(p.adjust(p_values, "BH") < alpha),
      sum(p.adjust(p_values, "BY") < alpha)
    )
  )
}

# Exemple d'utilisation
comparer_corrections(p_vals)

1 Non corrigé            10
2  Bonferroni             0
3        Holm             0
4    Hochberg             0
5      Hommel             0
6    BH (FDR)             0
7    BY (FDR)             0

title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
2.1 P-hACKing, P-hARKing
Two important concepts with p-values: - P-hacking : Manipulation of statistical analysis until an artificially low p-value below the defined \(\alpha\) threshold is obtained. Example: round the p-value ; lot of hypotheses testing without adjustment ; choose a data transformation to obtain a low p-value.

P-hARKing : Modify or establish new assumptions after seeing results.

In this section, we will focus on multiple testing to avoid one aspect of p-hacking. When multiple tests are performed simultaneously, the Family-Wise Error Rate increases, here is an illustrative example.
You are playing Russian roulette with a Smith & Wesson revolver, an 8-rounds revolver. Before each game, you spin the chamber and play:

1 time, the probability to die is \(1/8\) => 12.5%
2 times, the probability to die is \(1 - (1- 1/8)^2\) => ≈ 23.4%
10 times, the probability to die is \(1 - (1- 1/8)^{10}\) => ≈ 73.7%
30 times, the probability to die is \(1 - (1- 1/8)^{30}\) => ≈ 98.2%

title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
1.2 Student’s test (ou t test)
The Student’s t-test allows for a simple but important comparison: that of the means between two groups. The test statistic is defined as
\[
t = c \, \frac{\bar{m}_1 - \bar{m}_2}{s}
\]
With \(\bar{m}_1\) and \(\bar{m}_2\) are the means of the values in the two groups, \(c\) is a constant depending on the sample sizes, \(s\) is pooled standard deviation. \[
\bar{m}_1 = \frac{1}{n_1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} x_{1,i}
\qquad
\bar{m}_2 = \frac{1}{n_2} \sum_{i=1}^{n_2} x_{2,i}
\]
\(s_1^2\) and \(s_2^2\) are unbiased estimators of the intra-group variance.
\[
s_1^2 = \frac{1}{n_1 - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} (x_{1,i} - \bar{m}_1)^2
\qquad
s_2^2 = \frac{1}{n_2 - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_2} (x_{2,i} - \bar{m}_2)^2
\]
\[
s =
\sqrt{
\frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}
     {n_1 + n_2 - 2}
}
\]
\[
c = \sqrt{\frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}}
\]

1.2.1 Student two-sample test
Compare the means of two independent groups: trt2 (\(n=10\)) et crtl (\(n=10\)).
Assumptions:
The distributions of the two groups must be Normally distributed.







Figure 2: Data example of two groups.





tt <- with(exemple_data,
          t.test(weight[group =="ctrl"],
                 weight[group =="trt2"],
                 var.equal = TRUE))
tt

data:  weight[group == "ctrl"] and weight[group == "trt2"]
t = -2.134, df = 18, p-value = 0.04685
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.980338117 -0.007661883
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    5.032     5.526 


There is a difference between my two small sample groups. What would happen if we artificially increased the sample size by duplicating the data? I am keeping the same groups.





Figure 3: Graph showing the evolution of the p-value (log scale) as a function of sample size per group.







    Two Sample t-test

data:  weight[group == "ctrl"] and weight[group == "trt2"]
t = -7.0777, df = 198, p-value = 2.483e-11
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.6316394 -0.3563606
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    5.032     5.526 


In this example, I duplicated the dataset 10 times. We can see that the means are identical, but the associated p-value is much lower:

The statistical power associated with Student’s t-test depends on the sample size. The greater the number of observations, the more significant the results will be.

title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
1.3 Wilcoxon test

1.3.1 Wilcoxon two-sample test
The Wilcoxon two-sample test is a nonparametric test because no particular assumption is made to the distribution of the data, and it can be perform in very small sample size. The main idea of this test is to ranks all of the data and calculates the sum of the ranks for one of the groups. The null hypothesis \(H_0\) is that the two groups have identical distribution.
⚠️
One not correct thing about this test is it can be describe as a test for the median. This test can be use as a median test only if the distribution in the two groups is known to have the same shape.
⚠️
Test Statistic We will use \(SR\), the sum of the ranks of the group with the smallest sample size. \(n_{\min}\) is the minimum between group1 and group2 (and \(n_{\max}\) is the maximum between group1 and group2).

When \(n_{\min} < 10\):

\(C = SR - \frac{n_{\min}(n_{\min} + 1)}{2} \sim_{H_0} \text{centered Wilcoxon}(n_{\min}, n_{\max})\)


When \(n_{\min} > 10\):

\(SR\) is approximately Normally distributed:
\(SR \sim_{H_0} \mathcal{N}\!\left(\frac{n_{\min}(n_{\min} + n_{\max} + 1)}{2} \; ; \; \sqrt{\frac{n_{\max}}{6}\left(\frac{n_{\min}(n_{\min} + n_{\max} + 1)}{2}\right)}\right)\)
The test statistic \(U\) is:
\(U = \frac{SR - \frac{n_{\min}(n_{\min} + 1)}{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{n_{\max}}{6}\left(\frac{n_{\min}(n_{\min} + n_{\max} + 1)}{2}\right)}} \sim_{H_0} N(0, 1)\)

title: 1  General Theory of Statistical Tests
text:
Null hypothesis (H₀): The hypothesis submitted to statistical testing and considered true for the test, \(H_0\), is often a simple model or a defined value of a parameter. For example, there is no difference between the means of two groups. \(H_0\) : \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\)
Alternative hypothesis (H₁): hypothesis different from \(H_0\), commonly its opposite. Example \(H_1\): \(\mu_1 ≠ \mu_2\)



α Type I error (false positive): It is the probability to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true. In other words, it’s the risk of incorrectly concluding, based on the results obtained, that there is a real difference when in fact it is due to chance. Example: a player plays roulette, spins the wheel 6 times, and sees 4 red numbers and 2 black numbers come up. He concludes that there are twice as many red numbers as black numbers.








Figure 1: example of the roulette game





β Type II error (false negative): It’s the probability of not rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false. In other words, it is the risk of wrongly concluding that there is no difference when there is actually a difference.

1.4 Fisher’s Exact Test
Fisher’s exact test is a non-parametric statistical test used to assess the independence between two binary variables in a \(2×2\) contingency table. It is most commonly applied when the assumptions underlying \(\chi^2\) test and Yates’s \(\chi^2\) test are not valid. ️ ⚠️
This test assumes that the data are independent of each other, so care must be taken with statistical individuals (e.g., in single-cell data coming from the same patient).

\(H_0\): The two variables are independent
\(p_{abcd}\) is the probability that \(Y=a\) with n1, m1 and N known, fixed.
\(p_{abcd} = \mathbb{P}\!\left( Y = a \mid n1,\; m1,\; N \right)\)
\(Y \sim Hypergeometric(m1, N-m1, N)\)
So \(p_{abcd} = \dfrac{(a + b)! * (c + d)! *(a + c)! *(b + d)!}{a!* \, b!* \, c!* \, d!* \, n!}\)
To help to understand this probability, we will use numerical examples.

tab <- matrix(
  c(5, 8,   
    3, 15),  
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

colnames(tab) <- c("Smoke", "Dont_Smoke")
rownames(tab) <- c("less_than_49", "more_than_49")

print(tab)

fisher.test(tab)

## Manual computation of Fisher's exact test p-value

# Parameters fixed by the margins of the contingency table
# N  : total number of observations
# m1 : total number of Smokers
# n1 : total number of observations in less than 40yo

N  <- sum(tab)  
m1 <- sum(tab[, 1]) 
n1 <- sum(tab[1, ])   

## 1. Possible values of the random variable A

# A = number of smokers in Group < 40yo
# Under H0 (independence) and conditional on the margins,
# A follows a hypergeometric distribution.
#
# The admissible values of A are constrained by the margins:
#   0 <= A <= min(n1, m1)
# Here: 0 <= A <= 8

a_vals <- 0:m1


## 2. Hypergeometric probabilities

# For each possible value of A, compute the probability with dhyper():
probs <- dhyper(a_vals, m1, N - m1, n1)

## 3. Reconstruct all compatible 2x2 tables
# Each value of A uniquely determines a 2x2 table with the same margins:
# This allows us to explicitly list all possible tables considered
# in Fisher's exact test

fisher_table <- data.frame(
  a = a_vals,
  b = n1 - a_vals,
  c = m1 - a_vals,
  d = N - n1 - (m1 - a_vals),
  Probability = probs
)
print(fisher_table)

  a  b c  d  Probability
1 0 13 8 10 0.0055469040
2 1 12 7 11 0.0524434557
3 2 11 6 12 0.1835520949
4 3 10 5 13 0.3106266222
5 4  9 4 14 0.2773451984
6 5  8 3 15 0.1331256952
7 6  7 2 16 0.0332814238
8 7  6 1 17 0.0039154616
9 8  5 0 18 0.0001631442

## 4. Probability of the observed table
# In the observed data:
# a_obs = 5 
a_obs <- tab[1, 1]

p_obs <- dhyper(a_obs, m1, N - m1, n1)

## 5. Identify "as or more extreme" tables
# For the two-sided Fisher test,
# a table is considered at least as extreme as the observed one
# if its hypergeometric probability is less than or equal to
# the probability of the observed table.
fisher_table$Extreme <- fisher_table$Probability <= p_obs

## 6. Computation of the p-value
# The p-value is obtained by summing the probabilities
# of all tables classified as "extreme".
p_value_manual <- sum(fisher_table$Probability[fisher_table$Extreme])

test.pval <- fisher.test(tab)$p.value
print(paste0("Manual pvalue = ", p_value_manual,
             "Test pvalue = ", test.pval))
